slides.title: Function
slides.main: fn name(parameters) { body }; snake_case; declaration order doesn't matter.

captions: fn declares a function: a name, parentheses with parameters, a body in curly braces
Function and variable names use snake_case: say_hello, area_of_circle
You can call a function above where it is declared: the compiler reads the whole file

slides.title: Parameters
slides.main: Every parameter has a type; no default values.

captions: Every parameter has a type: fn greet(name: &str, times: u32)
The number and types of arguments must match — the compiler checks every call
No optional parameters or named arguments — one function does one thing

slides.title: Returning a value
slides.main: The result is the last expression without a semicolon.

captions: After the parentheses — an arrow and the result type: fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32
The result is the last expression of the body, with no semicolon and no return
Add ; — the expression becomes a statement, no result: expected i32, found ()

slides.title: Expressions and statements
slides.main: An expression yields a value; a statement doesn't; a block is an expression.

captions: An expression computes a value: 5, a + b, a function call, if, a block
A statement performs an action and gives no value: let y = 6;
A block {…} is also an expression: its value is the last line without ;

slides.title: return
slides.main: return is for early exit; don't write it at the end.

captions: return value; — leaves the function at once, for example on bad input
Checks at the start with return remove nested ifs and flatten the code
Don't write return at the very end of a function: an expression is enough

slides.title: () and !
slides.main: Without an arrow it returns (); the type ! belongs to expressions that never return.

captions: A function without -> returns () — the empty value, Rust's analogue of "nothing"
() is a real type with a single value; println!, assignment, and a block with ; give it
Type ! ("never") belongs to expressions that don't return: panic!, loop {}, exit — it fits any type

slides.title: Tuples
slides.main: Return a tuple; unpack with let (a, b); access with .0 and .1.

captions: Several values are returned as a tuple: fn divmod(a: i32, b: i32) -> (i32, i32)
let (q, r) = divmod(10, 3); — two variables at once, like a, b = f() in Python
pair.0 and pair.1 — access tuple elements by index with a dot

slides.title: if as an expression
slides.main: if–else returns a value; branches share a type; no ternary operator.

captions: if–else is an expression: the value of the branch that ran is taken
Branches must have one type; if without else returns () — no value to take
No ternary operator: if x > 0 { 1 } else { -1 } replaces it

slides.title: Recursion
slides.main: Stopping condition; call stack; nested functions.

captions: Recursion: fact(n) calls fact(n − 1); without a stopping condition the program crashes
Each call pushes a frame on the stack; very deep recursion is a stack overflow, and Rust doesn't guarantee tail-call optimization
A function can be declared inside another: it is visible only in that block and can't see its variables

slides.title: Passing by value
slides.main: Simple values are copied; a parameter can be made mut.

captions: Numbers, char and bool are passed by value: the function gets its own copy
You can change a parameter inside if you declare it mut: fn f(mut n: i32)
The caller's variable stays as it was — a reference lets a function change it (later)

slides.title: Macros
slides.main: The ! sign marks a macro; format!, panic!, assert!.

captions: println! with ! is a macro: it writes code at compile time and takes a varying number of arguments
format! returns a string instead of printing; panic! stops the program with a message
assert!(condition) and assert_eq!(a, b) fail if the check fails — the basis of tests

slides.title: After Python
slides.main: def → fn, types are required, no *args and no default values.

captions: def f(a): → fn f(a: i32) -> i32 { }; colon and indentation are replaced by curly braces
Types are required; result is the last expression; None → (); several values — a tuple
No default values, *args or **kwargs; lambdas are called closures — later
